# 182_Minimally_Invasive_Approaches_to_Colon_Cancer.qmd



## Overview

This chapter reviews minimally invasive surgery for colon cancer, mainly laparoscopic and robotic approaches, compared with open surgery. It concludes that minimally invasive surgery is safe and oncologically equivalent to open surgery when an equivalent cancer operation can be performed.

Key findings

- Short-term benefits of laparoscopy include shorter length of stay, earlier return of bowel function, and less pain/narcotic use, although operative times are generally longer.
- Robotic surgery offers technical advantages, but evidence over laparoscopy remains limited; it usually has longer operative times and higher costs.
- Long-term oncologic outcomes such as survival and recurrence are generally not different between laparoscopic and open surgery.
Additional topics

The chapter also discusses ERAS, intracorporeal vs extracorporeal anastomosis, CME, single-incision surgery, and practical operative pearls for right, left, sigmoid, transverse, splenic flexure, and total colectomy.


Slide 1 – Title

Minimally Invasive Approaches to Colon Cancer
Scope: laparoscopic, robotic, outcomes, costs, QoL, technical pearls

Slide 2 – Learning Objectives

Review evidence for minimally invasive colectomy
Compare open, laparoscopic, robotic approaches
Summarize key operative principles 
Slide 3 – Historical Background

First laparoscopic colectomy series reported in 1991
Early procedures: right hemicolectomy and sigmoid resection 
Slide 4 – Early Concerns

Cost and feasibility concerns
Trocar injury and oncologic safety concerns
Reports of port-site recurrence created caution 
Slide 5 – Randomized Trial Era

COST, COLOR, and CLASICC addressed major concerns
Established oncologic equivalence to open surgery 
Slide 6 – Why Laparoscopy Spread

Reduced length of stay
Earlier bowel recovery
Less pain and narcotic use 
Slide 7 – Database Support

National analyses confirmed fewer complications, transfusions, readmissions
Despite increased operative time and cost 
Slide 8 – Laparoscopic Learning Curve

Approximate proficiency: 55 right-sided and 62 left-sided resections 
Slide 9 – Robotic Surgery Introduction

Robotics as an extension of laparoscopy
Better optics, magnification, dexterity, ergonomics 
Slide 10 – Potential Robotic Advantages

May help with suturing, obesity, and difficult anatomy such as pelvis 
Slide 11 – Robotic Limitations

High-quality evidence remains limited
Cost and sustainability concerns
Some reports of increased iatrogenic complications 
Slide 12 – Robotic Learning Curve

About 75 cases initially
25–30 once a program is established 
Slide 13 – Core Principle

Minimally invasive surgery should be used only when safety and oncologic adequacy equal open surgery 
Slide 14 – Short-Term Outcomes Overview

Main comparisons: operative time, LOS, complications, conversion, node harvest 
Slide 15 – Operative Time: Lap vs Open

Laparoscopy consistently takes longer
Difference roughly 30–84 minutes 
Slide 16 – Conversion Rates

Range 3%–25%
CLASICC had highest rate; likely reflected learning curve 
Slide 17 – Robotic vs Laparoscopic Operative Time

Robotic operations generally even longer
Increase of 32–127 minutes reported 
Slide 18 – Robotic vs Laparoscopic Conversion

Usually no difference
Some studies showed lower conversion with robotics 
Slide 19 – Length of Stay: Lap vs Open

One of laparoscopy’s most consistent benefits
Reduction ranges from 1 to 5 days 
Slide 20 – ERAS and LOS

Fast-track/ERAS may blunt some LOS advantages of laparoscopy 
Slide 21 – LOS: Robotic vs Laparoscopic

Reported as similar or up to 2.25 days shorter with robotics
One study showed slightly longer LOS with robotics 
Slide 22 – Morbidity and Mortality

Most studies show no significant difference between approaches
Open generally has higher morbidity in three-way comparisons 
Slide 23 – Wound Infection Signal

Some laparoscopic studies showed fewer complications, largely due to fewer wound infections 
Slide 24 – Lymph Node Harvest

Usually no difference between lap/open or lap/robotic
Used as a surrogate for oncologic quality 
Slide 25 – Adequate Node Sampling

Minimum recommendation remains 12 lymph nodes
Laparoscopic and robotic approaches both support adequate harvest 
Slide 26 – Return of Bowel Function

Consistently earlier with laparoscopy than open surgery 
Slide 27 – Why Bowel Recovery Improves

Hypothesized from gentler tissue handling
May contribute to shorter LOS 
Slide 28 – Robotic Bowel Recovery

Ranges from no difference to 1.5 days better with robotics 
Slide 29 – Role of Intracorporeal Anastomosis

Robotic platform may ease intracorporeal anastomosis, potentially improving bowel recovery 
Slide 30 – Postoperative Pain

Laparoscopy generally reduces narcotic use versus open surgery 
Slide 31 – Clinical Importance of Less Narcotic Use

Especially relevant given pressure to reduce opioid prescribing 
Slide 32 – Robotic vs Laparoscopic Pain

No difference in pain scores in right colectomy trial 
Slide 33 – ERAS Overview

Designed to reduce perioperative complications and LOS 
Slide 34 – Evolution of ERAS

Colorectal-specific guidelines began in 2005
Updated 2019 recommendations include minimally invasive care 
Slide 35 – Same-Day Discharge

Feasible in selected colectomy patients within ERAS pathways 
Slide 36 – Same-Day Discharge Outcomes

Most patients discharged same day in reviewed pathways
Low leak and reoperation rates reported 
Slide 37 – Cost: Laparoscopic vs Open

Laparoscopy has higher operative and hospital costs
Driven by equipment and disposable instruments 
Slide 38 – Societal Cost Perspective

When time off work is included, total cost to society may be similar at 12 months 
Slide 39 – Cost: Robotic vs Laparoscopic

Robotic platform has consistently higher operative costs 
Slide 40 – How Robotic Costs May Be Offset

Lower LOS, fewer conversions, and fewer complications may narrow cost differences 
Slide 41 – Hidden Robotic Costs

Overhead and maintenance are important and often not fully captured 
Slide 42 – Long-Term Oncologic Outcomes

Across trials, laparoscopy is noninferior to open colectomy 
Slide 43 – Survival and Recurrence

No significant difference in overall survival, DFS, wound recurrence, or overall recurrence 
Slide 44 – Robotic Long-Term Outcomes

Limited data
Available studies show no survival difference among robotic, laparoscopic, and open approaches 
Slide 45 – Long-Term Hernia/SBO

Most studies show no clear difference between lap and open
LAFA showed lower hernia and adhesive SBO with laparoscopy 
Slide 46 – Extraction Site Matters

Midline extraction after laparoscopic-assisted colectomy linked to high incisional hernia rates
Off-midline extraction in robotics may help 
Slide 47 – Quality of Life

Most studies show at least some short-term QoL benefit with laparoscopy 
Slide 48 – Duration of QoL Benefit

Benefits are most notable in the first 6–12 months
Differences often fade over time 
Slide 49 – Robotic Surgery Summary

Compared with laparoscopy: higher cost, longer OR time, shorter LOS
Similar complications and reoperation rates 
Slide 50 – Sustainability

Robotic surgery generates more solid waste and greenhouse gases than laparoscopy 
Slide 51 – Intracorporeal vs Extracorporeal Anastomosis

ICA may reduce traction, allow suprapubic extraction, and improve bowel recovery 
Slide 52 – ICA Evidence

ICA often improves bowel recovery and may reduce wound issues
Usually does not shorten LOS 
Slide 53 – Complete Mesocolic Excision (CME)

Embryologic plane dissection with central vascular ligation
Intended to maximize mesocolic and nodal removal 
Slide 54 – CME Outcomes

Feasible and safe
Increases node yield
No clear oncologic benefit yet 
Slide 55 – Single-Incision Laparoscopic Colectomy

Feasible for selected patients
Similar outcomes to standard laparoscopy, sometimes shorter LOS 
Slide 56 – Technical Philosophy

Surgeons should know multiple dissection approaches
Anatomy knowledge is essential for safe oncologic surgery 
Slide 57 – Right Colectomy Pearls

Supine positioning
Medial-to-lateral approach emphasized
Protect duodenum and ureter
Off-midline extraction may reduce wound problems 
Slide 58 – Left/Sigmoid Colectomy Pearls

Left colectomy: medial-to-lateral approach
Sigmoid colectomy: lateral-to-medial approach with splenic flexure mobilization
Preserve ureter and autonomic nerves 
Slide 59 – Splenic Flexure and Transverse Tumors

Procedure depends on location
Segmental/left colectomy can be oncologically safe and may allow faster recovery than extended resection 
Slide 60 – Final Take-Home Messages

Minimally invasive colectomy is safe and feasible for colon cancer
Laparoscopy remains the dominant approach
Robotics is growing, but cost-effectiveness remains unproven
Technique should never compromise patient safety or oncologic quality
